This question has been before Parliament for many years, and it has been continually put off, presumably, as the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has said, through the influence of the express and railway companies. If that is so. then let us proceed with it now. Under the existing legislation it is possible to expand the parcel post we now have, as jthe hon. gentleman has himself admitted, by regulation of the Postmaster General. Even if we adopt this Bill, which legalizes parcel post, during the present session, I am quite willing to take it in its present form, and to leave it to the Postmaster General to develop a system under it. Probably you can get a better system without any special definition, and put it on the responsibility of the minister in office to develop and carry out a good parcel post system. There is no doubt that efforts are being made not only by the express companies, who will be injured by the establishment of a parcel post system, but by other interests throughout the country, to head off this proposal. Session after session I have observed the number of efforts which have been made to head off any legislation tending to establish a parcel post system. I have seen bogus petitions presented in this House, supposed to come from storekeepers in the country, which were certainly printed and circulated at the instigation of the express companies. That will be continued from session to session as long as this Parliament will permit it, and as long as measures of this



kind are dealt with towards the end of the session. I have been in this House now for twenty years, and I have observed that a great portion of each session has been taken up with the consideration of trade and constitutional questions, to the neglect of what I would designate as domestic questions. These domestic questions must be settled, but it would seem that we are now entering upon the consideration of another great constitutional question which may be detrimental to the consideration of the domestic questions to which I have referred, and which are of supreme importance.

The Postmaster General has not yet introduced his Bill, and when it is explained, I will state my position. What I have said has been based on what I have gathered of the Bill as it stands; perhaps I may change my opinion when it is introduced.

I said I was afraid ot the hon. gentleman's suggestion, because a suggestion of that kind, when the hon. gentleman is speaking on behalf of his party, might persuade the Postmaster General to drop the parcel post measure. I would be quite satisfied with some kind of a measure having the effect of expanding the parcel post system in this country. As I have said, my experience in this House is that the greater portion of the time of Parliament has been taken up with the consideration of constitutional and trade questions, to the neglect of important matters of domestic concern which should be settled. There always seems to be some matter which appeals to the people, and to which politicians resort, and in some way these domestic questions are placed in the background. I know as a matter of fact, that the railways of this country for forty years have delayed the building and enlarging of the canals of this co-untry, and they are to-day seeking to delay the establishment of a parcel post system. I hope the Postmaster General will go on with this measure. It really needs no legislation to expand our present system; even this Bill is not required. Under the existing powers vested in the Postmaster General in the regulations he has authority to make, he can expand the system of parcel delivery in respect of fourth-class matter, and in that way extend our present parcel post system. But this is a non-contentious measure; it simply adopts the principle and leaves to the Postmaster General the establishment of the rates and the regulation of other matters connected with the system. I would like to see these matters, as my hon. friend says, set out in the Bill, but for the present I would be satisfied with the Bill as it stands, and I am sure the Mr. MACLEAN (South York).
people of the country would be satisfied. We have been promised it now, and it has been explicitly promised this session. Almost every newspaper in the country expects it; the business interests and the people expect it, and now, at the tail end of the session, there is a suspicion that we are not going to have it.

Do you not want to
know the rates?

I would like to have
them, and I will stay here and try to make them.
That is what I want.

If we can get it, so much the better. If we are told that the Postmaster General is not in very good health, I shall be very glad to take this Bill, If the state of the country is such that the time of Parliament has to be taken up largely with major questions, these questions of the constitution, of defense, then I say it would be good policy for Parliament to have two sessions every year and devote one of those sessions absolutely to domestic questions. I think it would be a good thing, if this House must adjourn next week that we should have a fall session to deal absolutely with domestic questions, railway rates, parcel post and other questions which the people have at heart, and in reference to which they expect some kind of redress. Redress for public grievances is very slow in coming in this country. The people want lower express rates but they are getting them from the Railway Commission in only a very partial way. Parcel post will settle express rates the day after it is put in force. It has done that in the United States. It has increased the convenience of the people to ten times what it was when this business was under the control of the express company, it has cut the express rates away down, it has benefited business, it hurts no one and it has made a great monopoly understand that the people rule in the United States. We want them to know that the people rule in Canada and not the railway companies and if we have an organization right at hand, as we have in the post office, with an agent in every town and village, the framework is there for a splendid parcel post delivery that will give the people relief, that will encourage trade and give the railways to understand that they do not control this country. So I hope and trust that the Postmaster General will go on with this Bill and, if it cannot be made more definite this session, I will be quite willing to wait another session to get more details in the Bill. What the people of Canada to-day expect from the Postmaster General, and I learn this from conversations with members here and from reading the press of the country, is the in-

auguration of a parcel post system tomorrow or the next day or right away in order to give to the people of Canada the same convenience in regard to parcel post that the people of the United States and of all other civilized countries of the world have to-day. Why should Canada be so backward? Is it because the railway companies have the influence and the power to delay a reform of this kind? The people will be led to the conclusion that that is the reason. The late Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) ought to join with me in pressing on the minister the necessity of passing this Bill even in this session in order to put it into force. I am quite sure that he has the framework in his office for an enlarged parcel post system, and, with the experience of the United States, it ought to be no trouble to have a parcel post system working within thirty days. The country expects it and will insist on having it and it is the duty of the Government to give it.
In a Winnipeg newspaper of two days ago I read an article saying that the question of freight rates which for one reason or another are being postponed in this House and left to the Railway Commission is becoming ever more important. It says that unless that question is dealt with by Parliament it will become a question greater than the tariff and greater than the Naval Bill to the people of this country. Yet we can hardly get it up in this House, there is such pressure from questions like the Naval Bill and the discussion we had two years ago in regard to trade relations with the United States. We may now be on the eve of a great constitutional question in regard to the powers of the various branches of Parliament. If that is the case, my suggestion is that every year we ought to have two sessions or to divide the session in two and say that one half is devoted into dealing with these domestic questions.

I am sorry that in his remarks concerning the post office at Say-abec, the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), made the same charges that he made last session. He went over the same old history. He tried to show that the hon. the Postmaster General and the member for Rimouski had cut off the heads of a lot of Liberals in that county. I will relate the facts for his information. In 1896 I was the postmaster at Sayabec, having occupied that position since 1882. I began as a poor farmer, and acted as station agent at the same time. I grew up with the village, and I saw the village grow with me. As I was about the only educated man in the village, there being only a few settlers, I was asked to establish a post office. I did so, and I succeeded. After being postmaster for about 16 years, and having drawn a salary of ten dollars for the first few years, and kept that post office at a sacrifice for a long time, the party to which my hon. friend from Rouville belongs, came into power in 1896, and the second head that was cut off in the county of Rimouski was the head of Mr. H. Boulay. They did not take any time to make an investigation I asked for the reason of my dismissal, because it was something new in our country to have post offices changed with a change of Administration. It was something quite new, for during the Conservative Administration, extending over eighteen years, I knew a lot of Liberals who were postmasters, and the Conservative party never thought of dismissing them on account of their politics. Therefore, I had no idea that the party who came into power in 1896 would be so low as to cut off the heads of poor postmasters. But two or three weeks after they came into power, a post office inspector came to my residence and said: I want your papers. Dear 'Mr. Pelletier:
The Minister of Justice has asked me to reply to your letter to him of the IDth ultimo, with reference to the contract between your department and Miss Fawns. It is rather a difficult matter to advise you upon, as I find considerable difficulty in ascertaining what is the meaning and intention of the contract, and it is necessary to form some opinion about this before considering the question of the validity of the contract.
Having given it the best consideration I can, I am unable to find any clear ground on which the contract could be repudiated, although there are certainly particular points on which I do not think it could be supported. I will instance the provision in clause 11 that the Postmaster General is to be bound to issue a stamp-vending license to any person designated by the license. This seems to be clearly an - improper provision Mr. PELLETIER
where a government department is concerned, and one which must be against the public interest. Hooking .at the matter as a whole, I think in the opinion of tthe Government the contract is not a desirable one for your department to carry out; the most advisable course would be for you to give notice to the licensee that you do not intend to proceed further with the contract and leave her to take such action as she may be advised. I doubt whether any great harm can result from such a course of action. It .seems to^ me that if the licensee were to take proceedings for breach of contract she would ihave great difficulty in establishing serious damages. A considerable portion of the anticipated profit from these machines would seem to depend upon their capabilities for advertising and the sale of fancy notions, and I confess I can not see any apology for mixing up the business of the post office with such irrelevant projects.

I return the copy of the contract inclosed with your letter.
Yours faithfully,

On the ground that

introduction of a section into an Act of this Parliament could not have any effect whatever in regard to a provincially controlled railway. The hon. gentleman, I understand, is not asking to press his amendment?

This Bill is a little

I should tell this

At this late stage of the session, and in view of the fact that the Bill came from the Senate and was therefore apparently entitled to favourable consideration, the Railway Committee did not think it should assume the responsibility of killing the Bill. On the order being called for consideration of the message from the Senate insisting upon the adoption of the amendments made by them to Bill No. 97, respecting the Canadian Northern Branch Lines Company.-Mr. Sharpe (Lisgar).
Mr. LANCASTER. Stand.

Is there any way in
which the Chairman of the Railway Committee can arrange with the Senate to have this Bill passed? I heard a suggestion to hold a conference of representatives from both Houses to discuss it. I understand that the Canadian Northern would like to get the Bill passed, as part of one of the branch lines has been commenced. I have no doubt the people in the West would like to assist any road that will build branch lines. Is there any way of coming together?

As far as I can see, I think it is hopeless. This Bill, as drawn by the promoters, was absolutely in the proper form, the stereotyped form, the form that has had judicial interpretations by the courts. The amendment suggested by the Senate is not contended makes any change in the legislation. I am trying to speak respectfully, but they have a newfangled way of wanting to make this legislation which, in my humble opinion as a lawyer, throws a little doubt on the interpretation. I am not sure that it does, but I am afraid it might be so construed by the courts. On April 25 the matter was discussed and we were unanimous that we must adhere to our Bill and reject the amendment. The merit in our refusal and the absolute want of merit in the Senate's amendment is that the Senate does not contend that their amendment makes a bit of difference in the result of the legislation; but they say they would rather do it in that way. It is a very roundabout way, a very complicated way, a way that I admit as a lawyer may be open to a very different construction from the regular meaning of the Bill as it has been construed in other cases. The Senate's amendment fails to give a time for the completion of one of the branches already commenced. While they enact a new time for commencing as to the other lines, they do not perfectly describe them as we do in our Bill by reference to the particular charters. They fail utterly to state the new time for completion of the line already commenced, so that would be very bad legislation beyond any argument. I also point out that in their answer, which is a very complicated one, insisting on their amendment and insisting that the House adopt it, they admit that another amendment will still be necessary besides theirs to 'bring us back by this roundabout way to where we started by our plain and ordinary legislation. With the possible liability of being censured by this House for lack of dignity, I went to the Senate and tried to reason with these gentlemen that they should not send that report to this House, but should accept our suggestion and should not send to this House a message insisting upon an amendment of that kind in the face of our very clear language as to the result of it, which I shall again read to the House. It is true, I am the draftsman, but the House unanimously supported this message:
The amendment made by the Senate to the Bill No. 97, an Act respecting the Canadian Northern Branch Lines Company, was taken into consideration.
And the said amendment being read a second time;
Mr. Lancaster moved, that this Blouse do disagree with the Senate in the said amendment for the following reasons:-
Mr. NESBITT.
(a)	The said amendment does not fully describe the lines of railway referred to and tends to raise doubts as to the respective routes of the same.
(b)	The said amendment does not provide any limitation of time for completion of the first line of railway specified in section, 8 of chapter 56, of the Statutes of 1911, authorized by paragraph (a) of the said section.
Our Bill is so short and has such merit in its clear-cut language that I shall read it again:
The Canadian Northern Branch Lines Company may commence the construction of its lines of railway specified in section 8 of chapter 56 of statutes of 1911-
For the life of me I do not see how we could describe it better.
-excepting the first line which is already commenced, within two years after the passing of this Act.
-making the well-known and usual legislation. The answer given, which is before His Honour the Speaker, by a lot of language, tries to convince this House that their way of doing it, in a very long and not well-understood manner, will accomplish the same results, but suggests that if we do not think so we can pass a consequential amendment. Life is too short for me as Chairman of the Railway Committee and for the House to trouble with arguments of that kind from any Chamber, not pretending to say that our Bill does not do what both Houses intend and saying: If you do not like our amendment, you can pass another. They said also, in the informal conversation I had with them, that having insisted upon it, by their Railway Committee, they are going to insist upon it. It is unfortunate for the Tailway and probably for the people that this Bill cannot be passed this session. This House passed the Act in the ordinary way, but the other House admitting it is the usual and the understood way, with the desired result, interjects an unnecesssary amendment and asks us to try it for one year. I have been provoked into saying this and I think it is due to the House that I should say it. 1 cannot see much use in having a conference. If I was on the conference I could not give in. What we have done we have done in the proper way, and the Bill expresses what we both intended it should express. I say it is for them to give in, as they say they will not give in, the result will be that the Bill will have to go over for this session.
In what position will the railway company be, in the case where they have started grading on their railway?

They are all right as to that, because with this Bill not passing their other Act applies, and they have

three more years before them to complete that line. That line will be in shape, and we can renew the others next year. The [DOT]only point is as to whether they would have commenced any others sooner by getting the charter this ye'ar.

I have very great
respect for my hon. friend's knowledge ol the Railway Act and also for his very earnest work in the Railway Committee. I only want to know whether there is any way by which they could come together. I understand that the House is willing that the Bill should stand.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Anything to be done
would require to be done through a conference. The reasons for a conference must be prepared and assented to by this House. Rule 85 says:
When the House requests a conference with the Senate, the reasons to be given by this (House at the same shall be prepared and agreed to by the House before a message be sent therewith.
As the Senate has now adjourned until next week, perhaps it would be well to let this Bill stand, and if the promoters desire to provide for a conference, they would have an opportunity of doing so.
Progress reported.
Further consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 99, respecting the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway Company.

I wish to make a
motion in regard to this Bill. We considered these amendments in the Railway Committee, and it is quite evident that one of them is a mistake on the part of the Senate; in fact, I can say with certainty that it is, and that if we reject it no doubt they will withdraw it. If it were not so, they -would be undoing all the legislation passed by this House for several years, and would he interfering with the standard or model clause giving protection to municipalities. The first amendment made by the Senate is to strike out part of the route of the railway. As to that, the Railway Committee thought that they could not interfere so long as the promoters of the Bill were willing to accept the change. If the promoters of the Bill had insisted that they were entitled to have that part of their route into Montreal, as well as the rest of the route *proposed, I think we would have been inclined to say there is no reason why they should not have the right. But the promoters were willing to accept that amendment, and that being so, the legislative functions of this Parliament are not interfered with. The only result is that the promoters did not get so long a railway as they would otherwise have got. But the second amendment is one in regard to which this Parliament is'bound to protect the people. The Senate inserted in clause 7, the municipal clause of the Bill the word ' under ' in regard to poles and wires for telegraphing upon the highways. The standard municipal clause adopted by this House in regard to these matters gives the municipalities the control of the service, upon, along, or over the highways. They cannot go along or upon the highways without the consent of the municipalities, but of course they must be allowed to go under. If the municipal council will not allow them to do so, they can do so on the order of the Railway Commissioners, after investigation. If the word 'under' is inserted, the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission would be misted, and each municipality would be able to prevent a railway company, because its telegraph line must be part of the railway, from entering that municipality at all, and the Railway Commission would be helpless to interfere, even to allow the wires to go under the streets. So I move:
That this House do concur in the amendment made by the Senate to clause 2 of Bill No. 99, and do disagree with the Senate in its amendment made to clause 7, for the reason that the proposed amendment varies the well-considered standard section that ha9 been embodied in many railway Bills this session by both Houses, land would in effect transfer to municipalities the powers of the Board of Railway Commissioners to regulate the construction, operation and crossing under highways and public places with lines of wires when municipalities refuse to permit them to be placed upon along or across highways, in which event the powers to permit and regulate the crossing under these highways should, in the opinion of this House, remain in the Board of Railway Commissioners; and that a message he sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours therewith.
Motion agreed to.

Before six o'clock, I
think I had explained to the satisfaction of the committee that the present Postmaster General was not responsible for that part of his contract which the newspapers had been complaining about. An

effort has been made to try to confuse the two dates. I want to repeat, so that no mistake will be possible, that the contract in question, was signed by the Post Office Department on the 20t-h May, 1911.
Without an Order in Council.
Without an Order in Council, which makes it worse.
Which makes it void.

I would be glad if
the justice Department had been able to s-gree with that, but it is somewhat curious to see the hon. member for Rouville now calling his own contract null and void.
It is not my contract.
Who was the Postmaster General at the time?
I was.

Who was responsible for the contract from the point of view of responsibility to this House and the country? I may be very obtuse, but I say that it was the man at the head of the department. If some new constitutional Tule or theory can be propounded before the country which will upset all old-time constitutional rules, we will be very glad to hear what the hon. gentleman has to say about it, but this contract having been entered into by his department when he was Postmaster General, there is ns power on earth to relieve him from the responsibility, and I think that I am stating only a safe and sound principle in stating that.

Was the new contract,
which must have been passed with that Toronto firm, preceded by an Order in Council?
There is no new contract and my hon. friend cannot succeed in establishing that there was.

The first contract, I
understand, was with a party by the name of Katrine Ellen Fawns. The second contract was with the Dominion of Canada Postage Stamp Company, Limited, Toronto. Had my hon. friend an Order in Council for that?

It is of no use for
the hon. gentleman to try and draw a red herring across the trail. There is no first and second contract. There is only one contract, and that is the contract entered into when the hon. member was Postmaster General of Canada. That is the one and only contract, and that contract being to my mind a bad contract, I succeeded in obtaining certain amendments in favour of this country and in favour of the Post Office Department. It is no use try-Mr. PELLETIER.
ing to get out of it. I am asked: what does this new company have to do? The contract entered into by my hon. friend with Miss Katrine Ellen Fawns, a name he does not seem to remember now, because he has to read in the contract to find it, contained a most extraordinary clause in virtue of which Miss Fawns could transfer that contract without the consent of the Post Office Department at all. I have succeeded in securing an amendment to the contract so that now it cannot be transferred except with the consent of the Postmaster General. The company whose name appears now in the amendment, is the company to which this contract has been transferred in virtue of the clause put into the contract on the 20th May, 1911.

May I ask a question
of my hon. friend?

Just one minute; I
would like to finish this. It is not either pleasant or unpleasant for me to defend the worthy deputy minister of the Post Office Department, and it might appear strange to those who look at it from the point of view of politics; but I believe in standing by the officers of my department if I think they are right, whether they have been appointed by me or by my predecessors. The deputy minister has pointed out to me that it is very strange that the hon. member for Rouville repudiates this Miss Fawns and her boxes when a Bill was passed through this House in 1911, not by Dr. Goulter, who was not a member of the House, but by the hon. member for Rouville, and that Bill was passed for the express purpose of having this contract signed. I wonder if that statute is going to be repudiated also?

The statute is all
right, but the statement is not.

The contract could
not have been passed without that statute being passed first. It is not to me that the hon. member for Rouville will make a reproach for that. I was not his deputy minister, and never will be. This contract says, that stamp vending machines may be put at street corners. The Post Office Act did not allow that before. The Post Office Act provided, before this contract was entered into, that licenses for selling stamps should be revocable at the pleasure of the Postmaster General. That was a wise and safe provision because the Postmaster General should have the right to cancel such licenses at any time. That was the law, and this lady, under the contract which has been transferred now to this company, has the right to have these

stamp vending machines placed at certain corners for twenty years, or, if my hon. friend is right, for ten years. That is not revocable at pleasure, and the law was in the way. What do we find? We find that the hon. member for Rouville, then Postmaster General, had three short amendments made to the Post Office Act by this House. The first one is to add the words ' street stamp-vending boxes ' to the ordinary boxes which could be put in different places before. The second one is to add the words ' or for the sale of stamps or other post office supplies.' What is the third?
Paragraph ' o ' of the said sub-section of section- 9 is amended by striking out the words * revocable at pleasure.'
This statute completely removed all obstacles remaining in the way of the signing of the contract, the bill was assented to-mark the dates-on the 19th of May, 1911, and the contract was signed on the 20th May, the day after the statute had been assented to. Here is a gentleman who says that he knew nothing of that contract. I invite hon. members to put all these facts together and judge for themselves. It is unfortunate, but we have a difference here between the word of the hon. member for Rouville and the word of the deputy postmaster general. I am not concerned with the quarrel between the hon. member for Rouville and the deputy postmaster genefal, but 1 am bound to put the facts before the committee in justice to my deputy minister. These are the facts. I had some reason to be surprised when, for the last two or three days in succession, the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has stated here in my absence that we should not have stamp vending machines with advertisements on the streets. You know the reason why, now. One of the amendments which I have succeeded in obtaining provides that these machines will not be put everywhere at the sweet will of Miss Fawns and her representatives, but that the Postmaster General will have to give his consent to the erection of any of these machines. The Postmaster General will see to it that this contract is not abused, and that the machines are not put in such places as will hurt the public interest and the interest of the cities or of the municipalities.

How do the machines
work?
They are not in operation yet.

Ask
Miss Fawns.

I know Miss Fawns well.
I would like to ask the hon. Postmaster
360	[DOT]
General how the machines" are working, and if they are giving satisfaction.

I know they are. I
know the machines.

My hon. friend makes light of all this. I may tell him, and in the presence of the deputy Postmaster General, that I never saw Miss Fawns and never spoke to her. That is the truth.

in council, and therefore I am not bound by that contract. That is the law.

My hon. friend seems to be under a very extraordinary misapprehension. He says:	This contract is
null and void; just cancel the contract.
I may tell my hon. friend that I did all I could, without, of course, breaking faith with the parties who signed this contract

speechtext: I should remind the hon.., gentleman that he ought not to interrupt.

I have practiced more than you have.

You are putting yourself in the wrong by being so excited. When a man is in the hole, he should stay still. The more he moves the earth around him, the more he goes down. Which I had not made.

The hon. gentleman

Who was the Postmaster General when the contract was made?

Hon. Rodolphe
Lemieux. I was not here, but that is what I was told.

-that any matter relating to the Post Office Department might be brought under discussion, and the discussion went on on that basis.
The subject was introduced-
Just a moment. I am interested in the quarrel between the Postmaster General and his predecessor. But I am entitled to have the discussion confined to what is before the Chair.

I can tell mv hon.
friend that parcel post is part of the Post Office Department policy which we are now discussing.	'
But the Bill is not before the Chair. It is not yet introduced.

Oh, yes. It is printed and distributed. The hon. gentleman does not look at his files every morning. But I quite understand the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton North. In friendly feeling toward the hon. member for Rouville, he thinks we should talk of something else, because he finds there has been enough for that hon. gentleman to swallow for one night.

If the hon. Postmaster General has any observations to make concerning the member for Cape Breton North, he will find that the member for Cape Breton North is quite capable of looking after himself any day of the week.
Do not get mad. Remember the dignity and traditions of an old-time judge.

I desire to make an appeal to the Postmaster General on this subject. I am sure that, with the rest of the committee, I have enjoyed very much the discussion hitherto; but I think the Postmaster General, perhaps, will see that

to enter into a full discussion of the parcel post matter would not save the time of the committee or promote the early prorogation which, I am sure, he equally with a number of us, very much desires. I do not raise a point of order, but I appeal to him whether it is not a little irregular on the estimates to discuss parcel post about which we should get into a further discussion. It will open up the whole subject of parcel post and any of us might wish to make a speech on this important question. I put that to him in the most friendly spirit, without participating in the quarrel between himself and the hon. member for Rouville.

I take the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer, who is always very fair, in the spirit in which they are made. I myself am one of those who desire to see prorogation come. I would not have alluded to this matter at all but for the fact that the hon. member for Rouville spoke about it this afternoon, and I thought I might say a few words in answer. But there is a good deal in the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer, and I shall not say more about this now than to recall to the House the fact that under the law as it stands, I have, as Postmaster General, all the power to fix the rates which my hon. friend from Rouville says I should ask of this House in detail. That is my point.

I wish the
minister to understand that I do not want to interfere with his right to reply to criticism. That is the right of every member. But I, in fairness, desire to recall the fact that what the hon. member for Rouville said was that from his point of view-and I think he made it personal-the measure was controversial.

But he gives the
*reason for the measure being controversial -that the rates are not given in the Bill. My answer is that I have the power to fix these rates now. Whilst there is at present a law authorizing parcel post, some additional legislation is necessary in order to effect the results at which we are aiming. It really is not new legislation; it is but a remodelling of the old law, and it has been one of my most earnest desires to give this boon to the Canadian people. If the Opposition will help me to pass this Bill and to receive the unanimous consent of Parliament for its adoption, my hand will be much strengthened when I come to deal with the express companies ajnd everyone concerned. Fresh from Parliament with power given to me unanimously by this Parliament, I think I could overcome all those obstacles which now seem to be almost insuperable. Of course I am not going to insist upon it at this stage of the session, but if after Mr. CLARK (Red Deerl
looking over the Bill, having particular regard to section 74 of the Post Office Act, the hon. member for Rouville and other hon. gentlemen of this House come to the conclusion that the matter is not controversial, I will be prepared to put it through and to inaugurate in a few months this great public service for the benefit of the people of this country.

The committee will
realize that with the exception of a few moments devoted on a Wednesday evening to the one-sixth vote, this is the first occasion since the beginning of this long session upon which we have had an opportunity of discussing* matters in connection with the Post Office Department, and I thought it was my duty as a member of this House to deal with these different matters at this stage.

I am sure my hon.
friend will give me credit for being the last one who would oppose any such action. I have told him that he is at liberty to discuss these matters fully. My hon. friend has spoken about the Wireless Bill; let me say a few words about that. This Bill is one which has for its object the breaking of the backbone of the cable monopoly. I know that very powerful interests are now fighting against the passage of this Bill, which is the result of the work I did in England last summer. If the majority is in favour of this Bill-whether or not it would be thrown out elsewhere I am unable to say-I think it would be regrettable if we were to miss this opportunity of encouraging any competition that will have the effect of reducing the tremendously high rates which the people of Canada are now paying.
My hon. friend referred also to mail bag locks. We have heard a few things in this House about these locks, and outside of the House people have continued to speak of the purchase of 350,000 locks, when they know that that is not true. Some of the newspapers are edited by men who, I am sure, are descendants of .Ananias, although Ananias would surely feel that he was outstripped by these people to-day. Of course they consider it to be part of their duty, and I do not mind it, for I have been through the mill before, but my experience has been that the caluminators never succeed in the end. We have been told that these locks are first-class. Now the hon. member for Rouville says that the locks were not so good as he thought; that there were some bars which had been ordered, and which would have made the locks very good, had not the unfortunate Postmaster General cancelled the order for the bars. My hon. friend, is in the same dilemma as he was in respect of the contract of May, 1911.

The less said about
these locks the better for you.

I do not hesitate to
speak of them; I have no reason to be ashamed. I made a good contract, and yet the hon. gentleman stands up in his seat and tries to cast aspersions upon my conduct. He has been invited to repeat them to this House; he has not done so, and he will not do so. My hon. friend has read the letter cancelling the order for these bars. The bars are necessary for the new locks as well as for the old. We gave an order in September, 1912, and six months afterwards the order had not been filled. We wanted these bars, and we cancelled the order. Where is the business man who, after giving an order for something which he wanted, apd waiting for six months without receiving that which he ordered, would not cancel the order and endeavour to get the goods elsewhere? That is what I did. Information has come to the department that Mr. Lapointe, who has the patent for these bars, is probably not entitled to that patent. I am making these remarks to prove'to the hon. member for Rouville that the cancellation of the order for the bars was not done on account of any discussion which took place in this House. In order to get the bars which we want in the department we have called for tenders. The people who have tendered have asked us a very large price on account of the risk they run in respect of the patent, but I hope that before long we will get them at a more reasonable price.
My hon. friend has spoken about rural mail, and asked me to give him some information in that regard. I may say that the number of routes authorized up to October, 1911, 614. The number of boxes was 16,015. Since the present Government 'came into power, 720 new routes and 185 extensions of old routes have been authorized. The number of routes authorized to-'day is 1,385; number of boxes reported erected, 44,010; number of boxes which will be erected when the routes now under advertisement, for tenders go into operation, 14,800; number of boxes which will be erected on routes already authorized, but not yet in operation, 9,800. The number of boxes which have been erected after the roads have been in operation for some time, which must be considered in addition to above figures, approximately 3,000. That makes a total of 71,610.	55,000 boxes have been erected
since October, 1911, against 16,015 erected by the previous Government. That, I think, is the information asked for by the hon. member for Rouville. If he wants more information I shall be glad to try and get it for him.

I understand that Quebec makes a very poor showing in connection with this service-that there are few roads there as compared with Ontario. Has any step been taken by the department to point out the advantages of the rural mail service so that it may be introduced more extensively in Quebec? I understand that there is a large number of constituencies, probably more than one half of those in the province, if not two-thirds, that have no such service at all.

The hon. member is right. The banner province, so far as rural mail is concerned, is Ontario. But very close to it, and neck and neck in the run, is the little province of Prince Edward Island. There is much less interest taken in this particular matter by the other provinces and in the province of Quebec they do not seem to have so far appreciated the benefit coming from this rural mail delivery. I have lost no opportunity to induce our people to try it. _ I have given an example In my own riding. Of course, it is a matter in which the Government does not come forward and install the boxes of its own motion; there must be a demand for them, and the demand must come from fifty-one per cent of the people on the route which the rural mail will follow.-This was, to a certain extent, unknown in the province. I inaugurated two or three routes in my constituency and had, some difficulty in bringing it about. I may say that now the people who have seen the benefit of it are coming in and joining the procession and asking for boxes. I have tried it elsewhere. I have tried it in the good old Liberal parish in which I was born. I have said to them thpre:	Why
should you not try this? ana they have tried it. I have asked other parts of the province to . do the same thing, and I expect they will come in and join in the expenditure which we have been making. In one respect that will give us time to breathe. We are' now giving the rural mail delivery to people who are anxious to have it; others will learn about it later and their turn will come.

Has the department a circular that could be distributed in some of these constituencies showing the advantage. I am sorry to say that in my own constituency the benefits of the service are unknown. I would like to point it out to the people, but I am not thoroughly familiar with it myself. If the department had a circular that could be given to persons applying for it, it would be a way to introduce the system.
We have not issued any circulars because the demands are very numerous and we have not needed to invite people to come in.
You have booklets and blank forms in both languages.

I shall put it very
' briefly for my hon. friend for Bonaventure, and then he will know all about it except the details which are not necessary to know. You have fifty-one per cent of the farmers or people living along a certain route who will sign a petition to the inspector of the inspectoral division asking for the establishment of a rural mail route. When that is fyled in the office a member of the post office inspector's staff goes down, examines the locality and locates the route according to the regulations of the department. There the whole thing is done. The only liability on those signing is that each patron undertakes to purchase, the box, which costs $3. I have allowed two patrons to join in the same box. My experience has been that that arrangement does not last long, the two patrons say:	Now
we know everything about this, we want one each, our own box. The box is adapted to give certain indications. If there is anything in the box for the courier to take up, the box is set in a certain position. If the courier puts something into the box he places it in another position and the people in the house can see that there is something for them and the boy or girl goes to the box. The payment of $3 is once for all, then the box belongs to the man who purchases it. The upshot of the whole thing is that every man has got a post office at his door. The courier has with him booklets of stamps and he sells the stamps to the farmers so that they have at home all of the postal facilities they require. More than, that, they have the right to receive registered mail from the courier and give him registered mail. It amounts to this that it is a small post office at the door of every farmer in the country.
Would the parcel post be applied to this service.
That is a big question, it is an obstacle in our way. The boxes are too small to include parcel post.
Would the courier accept parcel mail?

Of course he will, but it will become a question of price. He has contracted under certain conditions to carry certain mails. If the weight is doubled, we may expect some complaint for an increase in price, but we shall try to do our best.
Does not the minister think that the percentage of fifty-one per cent on the route is too high?
No.

In my own county I found sometimes that it was difficult to get that Mr. PELLETIER.
many to take the boxes at $3 each whereas if the percentage was reduced to say twenty-five per cent then they could start the route and others would be likely to come in later on; like the measles, it would be catching. I have always thought that the percentage of fifty-one per cent of the people living on the proposed mail route was too high. Is it the custom of the Post Office Department to close the post offices on the rural mail routes? I find some opposition to that, the people do not like to have the post offices closed, and as the postmaster gets only $35 a year, it does not involve a heavy expense on the Post Office Department. I was glad to hear him say he intended to raise the minimum salaries of postmasters.

The two questions go one with the other; they are very closely connected. If we were to lower that minimum to 25 per cent we would not be able to close the small post offices which now exist along the mail routes, because 75 per cent of the people would still have to deal with the post office. The policy of the department is, at every point, where possible, to do away with the small office, and to deliver the mail to everybody under the rural mail system. We find now that we have our hands full with the 51 per cent minimum, and I do not hesitate to say- this is no reflection on anybody-that where there is only 25 per cent of the people, we had better wait until we have 51 per cent.

But when a rural mail delivery is established on a certain section, and the post office is closed, and several people in that section are too poor to pay $3 for the boxes, those people are absolutely debarred from post office privileges. I think it is a great mistake to close these post offices simply because of the rural mail delivery. I am really surprised to hear the Postmaster General say there are so many applications that they cannot be filled.
What percentage of people on a mail route must avail themselves of the rural mail delivery before the Postmaster General proceeds to close the office?

The rule is that we
close the local office when the rural mail is established. We have to make some exceptions sometimes, but we hate to make them, and we only do so in special cases.

Is the
system found to work as well in sparsely settled districts as in thickly settled districts, and how many people to the mile

are necessary before the route is established?

It works infinitely
better in thickly settled parts.
Is any number of people to the mile required?

It is not necessary
that there should be any number to the mile provided there are 51 per cent of the people living on the route.
Did I understand the Postmaster General to say that these mail routes cannot be established except on existing mail routes?

That was the old
policy, and it has been changed. We establish mail routes now wherever they are asked and where, in the opinion of the branch of the department, the local conditions justify them.

What would the Postmaster General do in the case of a long *mail route, say 60 miles in length, where the work is performed by one contractor? There might be places along the route where the settlement is not thick enough 'to justify a rural mail system. Would he break up the mail contract and adapt him-.self to the circumstances of the country?

We give notice to
the contractor, but we do not establish *mail routes so long as that. They have to be established in such a way that the same courier is able to go over the whole route in a comparatively short time and do it regularly, so that the people know the hour at which the courier will reach a certain point. The courier does his best in that respect, but of course he is not always on time, especially when the roads are bad in winter.

Is the remuneration to the
courier the same, one dollar per box?

The courier gets a
dollar per box, and the department pays that. The local man, the farmer, has only got to pay the price of his box, and he gets the service for nothing. I think I have covered pretty well all the remarks made by my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr, Lemieux). but there is the matter of newspaper postage which was touched upon by my hon. friend from South York. I may inform him that the department is at work on this question, and I think I may say that what he has said this afternoon will help us in the good work we are trying to do. I do not believe that the PostOffice Department should carry newspapers which are only for advertising purposes or something of that kind at the price we are .carrying them now. I do not want to go
into more details just now. This matter is at present under consideration in the department.

I understand that
the department has fixed the allowance to the courier at $30 per mile over the route that he has to go, that is to say, if it is a twenty mile route, he will get $600, and, in addition, a dollar for each box on the route. If the courier can succeed in increasing the number of boxes on his route, he will get so many more dollars. That dollar is paid by the department, and the farmer pays nothing except $3 for his box.
I am under the apprehension that the minister will have to increase that allowance of $30 per mile. No doubt he has succeeded already in getting a good many couriers to undertake the work for $30 per mile, but the complaints are somewhat serious, and I have the impression that when the time comes to renew those contracts he will find himself unable to do so. The demand will be for more money, because the consideration is certainly too small. If the parcel post branch is to be added, he will have to add a good deal more to the remuneration which the courier gets for his work.
I wish to warn the minister, because my experience in the country is that there is serious complaint as to this remuneration of $30 per mile, and I fear that either he will have to increase the remuneration or we will have to go back to the old system. In my county we have perhaps eight or ten routes opened up. The minister will remember that in one case he advertised for tenders and the lowest was $900, in fact it was the only tender. I wrote and asked the man whether he was aware that he would get $1 per box in addition? He was not aware of that fact, but he said that -in view of that extra amount he would reduce his tender by $100. The then minister refused to enter into a contract because the tender exceeded the rate of $30 per mile. The result was that the route has not been opened up, although there was an urgent demand for it. I believe the minister has consented to make a special case of that for reasons which I explained to him, namely, bad roads and hilly roads. There are conditions that must be taken into consideration. You cannot have an *absolute rule for all routes because some are much more difficult to travel over than others. I think that the route I referred to is a route of only about 20 or 22 miles and, if not in operation now, will be in operation in a day or two, and the people are very grateful for it. In regard to the closing of offices, a question has arisen as to the closing of the leading office on that particular route. I asked a gentleman who lives close to one of the post offices, because there are three, if it

would inconvenience the (people if that post office were closed. 1 had an apprehension that it would. This gentleman made a careful calculation and he discovered that there Were only a few people who would not be supplied by the rural mail delivery, and for the sake of these people he desired that the office should not be closed at once. The department have very kindly agreed that they will keep that office open until we advise them that the people will be able to get accommodation in one way or another. I think they will he perhaps in a few weeks or few months. At any rate, the people of the country will have to be very considerate and assist the department in bringing about this rural mail delivery if it is going to be a success. I found that the better plan was to have a man from the inspector's office in Toronto go out into the township and assist the people in laying out their routes, have the boxes subscribed for and then call for tenders. They are getting along very well. There is serious complaint about the small consideration that is being allowed the couriers. It is kept down to $30 per mile. I'feel assured that the minister will have to pay a little more liberally at the expiration of four years if he is going to have these couriers extend their contracts. The people must take an interest in it; otherwise the Government would hardly be able to carry it on.

The average length
of the rural mail routes is 25 miles. The rates of $30 per mile is not a hard and fast rule. My hon. friend and I have had to fight about that matter.
We had a good fight too, and I got the best of the hon. gentleman.

Yes, we fought like
friends, I fighting to reduce the price in the interest of the public and my hon. friend fighting to have his electors given a better price. I thought we were doing wha't was reasonable, and I found my hon. friend very reasonable. His case was a special one.
Yes, the mountain road.

We made inquiry
about what my hon. friend told me-his word is as good as his bond-'and we were able to agree in the end. We are trying to keep down the price as much as we can, because the increase in the expenditure for this rural mail delivery is going to be very heavy, and we cut every dollar that we possibly can.

Are not the mail delivery
routes put up to tender and contract?
Mr. HENDERSON.
Yes.

Does not the minister
find that there are contracts on a lot of routes at a good deal less than $36 per mile.

Very rarely. It is
oftener above. In some cases it is as my hon. friend states. We find that in some cases people will tender at $15 a mile, but that does not happen very often. That usually happens in the case of a man who wants to get- the contract at any price and be able to look at the other man and say: I got the contract over your head. We generally give him the contract, if he is responsible, and he is stuck in the end.
Have you ever raised the price after the contract has been entered into?
Not as a rule.
Is the contractor obliged to carry out the contract?

Sometimes his securities will write to the department and say that they do not wish to continue their bonds and we will have endless trouble about it. In some cases we consent to cancel these contracts, but we keep the contractor to his contract as long as we can do so without losing money.

Call for new tenders
if the amount is over $200.

It is only decent that I
should say that the rural mail delivery system has worked remarkably well wherever it has been tried. There are little troubles sometimes, and the minister is doing the best he can to overcome them. All these little things will arise, and if members who talk about them will look into the matter, they will find they can overcome them. I think the service is getting on remarkably well considering the time it has been in existence.

I am glad to hear
that, and I think there is occasion to pay a compliment to the very good man that we have at the head of the branch and who is doing his work well.

What
has been the fate of the application made for a rural mail delivery service between Merigoniish and Malignant Cove, and why has no contract been entered into for the carrying of the mail there?

The superintendent
of the branch tells me that the route is so long that it would be difficult to have the contract carried out unless the contractor travelled at night.

Has any contract
been entered into for the carrying of the mail between Merigonish and Malignant Cove, if so, what is the amount, and who is the tenderer?

I am not able to give my hon. friend that information at the present moment. The superintendent will have to look into the matter, and I will have the information for my hon. friend at the next sitting.

Perhaps, in view of
the remark which the Postmaster General has made, I might get the information if I called at the department on some later occasion?
Certainly.

Tenders were called
some time ago and the contract was not awarded. I was given to understand that it was under consideration for some reason. Why has the contract not been awarded?

My hon. friend will
be *welcomed by Mr. Bolduc, the head of the branch, if the contract has been awarded. If the contract has not been awarded, the policy of the department is to keep these matters secret until the contract has been awarded.
May I ask the minister if he is going to cut this route into two?
We will have to give the hon. gentleman the information.

With reference to
that particular mail route, a proposition was made to divide the route as it at present exists between Merigondsh and Malignant Cove for the purpose of rural mail delivery at a place called Lismore ot Knoydart. I would like if the minister would give the information to my hon. friend from Antigonish, and in this way advise me in regard to this particular phase of it.
Yes, when the matter is closed un, the superintendent of the branch will give the information to the hon. member for Pictou as well as the hon. member for Antigonish.

As the superintendent
is here, perhaps my hon. friend could inform me as to the cause of the delay in putting into operation the rural mail service between Daniston and the city of Ottawa, in the county of Russell, i understand that the contracts were received nearly two months ago, that everything was regular and that the people were.given to understand that the route would be put into operation at an early date. That has
not been done. Could the minister give me the reason?
Mr. PELLETIER [DOT] The superintendent informs me it is because the tenders are too high.

Will new tenders be
invited?

In such cases the inspector is entrusted with the task of trying to find, either from the men who have tendered or from somebody else, somebody who will take the contract at a lower price. The policy of the department is to write the local inspector, who then tries to get a price which the department can pay.

I am glad to get this explanation from my hon. friend, because a great many people in my constituency are under the impression that the gentleman who was my oponent in the last election was the cause of the delay. I am glad to find that their suspicions are unfounded.
The hon. member for Russell should not complain, because his county has been well treated.
I have no complaint in this regard.

The hon. member for
Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has referred to Colonel Bourke, who was dismissed. It is true that I received a recommendation of Colonel Bourke from the hon. Minister of Militia (Mr. Hughes), and I put this recommendation before the member for the county (Mr. Lamarche). The hon. member for the county told me that to his personal knowledge this gentleman had taken an active part in politics. It is a well-known rule, adopted by both parties, that when an hon. member says that to his personal knowledge this has been done, his -word is accepted. I have followed that rule in this case.

Last night I made a few allusions to dismissals in my county. I did not ask for any mercy for any of them. They have taken their medicine as best they could. I would like the hon. minister, however, to look into one case, that of a woman who was dismissed, Madame Mar-cotte, of Nouvelle West, Bonaventure. She is a deserving woman with a large family, and has kept this office for a number of years. It was formerly held by her husband.
The deputy minister is making a note of it.

In regard to Colonel Bourke, the minister says that the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Lamarche) in-

sisted on the dismissal of Colonel Bourke, on the ground that he had personal knowledge of his admixture in politics. When .stating the case this afternoon, I forgot to read a letter from the hon Minister of Militia, under date of July 18, 1912. This is the letter:
My Dear Colleague,-I am in receipt of a communication from Colonel L. P. H. Bourke, -commanding the 80th Nicolet Regiment in which he states that some person is working to have him removed from his position as railway mail clerk, on the ground that he took an active part in politics.
I have made inquiry and find that this officer has not taken any part in politics, and I would respectfully request that, before he is dismissed from his position as a railway mail clerk, full inquiry should be made in connection with the matter.
I may say that so far as his military record is concerned, it is of the best.
Please have a full inquiry made into this matter, and oblige.
Faithfully,
(Sgd.) Bam. Hughes.
I do not know whether an investigation was held.. Colonel Bourke says that there was no investigation; but Mr. Lamarche, who ran as a Nationalist candidate in the .county of Nicolet, exacted from the hon. Postmaster General that this gentleman should be dismissed, in- spite of the recommendation of the hon. Minister of Militia. I leave the people to judge of the facts.

In regard to the rural mail routes, it is pretty clear that the present system is not suitable in the case of long routes. Some new system ought to be adopted that will give better service in localities of that character. They are generally localities which have not the ad-wantage of railway communication. As the -minister is anxious to do his best for the -country districts, I would suggest to him the importance of providing that automobiles should be used on these long routes. The post offices might be put a little closer together than they are in some places; and, by the use of automobiles, parties living a long distance from the railways would have the advantage of quick delivery of their mail. I have a number of such cases in my own constituency. There is one case where the mail has to be carried from the station of Heatherton to the town of Canso, .a distance of sixty miles. There are other cases, such as from Antigonish to Sherbrooke, a distance of forty miles, and from Antigonish to Isaacs harbour, also about forty miles. These are very good roads; and in the summer season the trip could be made in two or three hours with an automobile, whereas by the slow coach service which we have at the present time *delay occurs, and the people on these routes Mr. LEMIEUX.	i
do not get their mail from Halifax until late in the night or perhaps the next morning. In the winter season, there might be difficulty about using' automobiles; but I think, with a little extra amount put in the estimates for accommodating these places, the hon. minister could do a great deal towards improving the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: How would automobiles do in the winter season?

I understand that automobiles are run successfully through the snow in many cases; and, in a winter like the last one, I do not think there would be any trouble. Horses could be used in the winter season, if necessary. Livery men find plenty of use for their horses in the summer, but it would suit them very well if we used automobiles in the summer and horses in the winter, because that is the time when they have little use for their horses for other purposes.
I wish to protest against the hon. minister assuming the right, as I understand he does, to cancel mail contracts. I submit that he should not cancel a mail contract that has been obtained through fair competition in the open market. If a contract has been obtained by political favour, through the recommendation of some politician, I would have no objection to the minister cancelling it if he sees fit. That, however, is not the kind of case to which I refer. I refer to cases wjhere advertisements are placed in the newspapers; where tenders are asked for; where a number of people submit tenders and where the lowest tenderer secures the contract. After having secured the contract, he goes to a great deal of expense in order to carry it out properly. He has to obtain horses and coaches; he has to find bondsmen that he wiil carry out his contract for four years. The contract is signed. An election comes along and the administration is changed. A new Postmaster General takes the place of the old one; and he assumes the right to cancel the contract, and turns the man adrift. This man accordingly loses a large amount of money. I have a case of this kind in my mind. I understand the minister has disregarded these contracts altogether. A number of cases have occurred throughout this country in which that has been done. Questions have been asked in the House during the present session, and I was very much surprised to hear the hon. minister give the reason that the contracts contain a clause that enables the Postmaster General to cancel it when he sees fit. Everybody knows that that is an ordinary clause in Government contracts. I shall not find any particular fault with the Postmaster General for the dismissals in the constituency of Humboldt, because I know there have been a certain number of them, and I would not undertake to say in all cases that if political partisanship is a fault that is deserving of the penalty of dismissal, some of those dismissed were not rightly dismissed. My complaint is with reference to the way in which the post office service at a particular point in that constituency which I have the honour to represent was held up for practically a whole year awaiting the decision and the redecision of the defeated candidate in that constituency in the recent election as to who should be appointed to fill the vacancy as postmaster. I refer to the case of the village of Wakaw, a new village on a branch line of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Young to Prince Albert. The steel was laid into this point some time in the fall of 1911 and immediately a small village sprang up, as they do in the West very quickly. The old post office was some three-quarters of a mile away. It became necessary at once, as the former postmaster had a business at the point where he was, that the post office should be removed for the convenience of the tillage. The matter was brought to the attention of the department, according to a file which was brought down in the Senate pursuant to an order dated February of this year:
Fo.r a return of all papers, telegrams, petitions, letters and other documents in any way-referring to the appointing of Mr. McCloskey as postmaster at Wakaw, Sask.
In February of last year a widow woman supporting herself by keeping a boarding house or restaurant in the village applied for the position of postmistress, and she accompanied the request with a petition signed by all the citizens of the village that she should be appointed. The matter was referred to the defeated candidate at the last election, Mr. Hearn, and he recommended this woman's appointment as postmistress. I have no fault to find with the course of the department in referring this recommendation to the defeated candidate, I understand that is the recognized practice, but I do find this fault that to suit the views and change of views of the defeated candidate, the public service in this particular village was a disgrace for the whole of last year, the service was absolutely unsatisfactory from every standpoint to the citizens, and, notwithstanding protest after protest which was made to Mr. SINCLAIR.
the department over the delay in the change of the post office and the appointment of a postmaster, and with reference to the character of the person to be appointed, the minister deliberately awaited the pleasure and the will of the defeated candidate and kept the people at this point with the most inefficient and inadequate service through the whole of 1912. As I say, in February, the petition of the citizens to have this woman appointed, was signed, and in April-I suppose the department had inquired whether this would be a proper appointment or not- Mr. Hearn wrote to the department that this woman should be appointed. Later in April, Mr. Hearn changed his recommendation, and recommended that a man by the name of McCloskey, who at the time was teaching a school a few miles from the village, should be appointed, the understanding being that Mr. McCloskey was likely to move into the village. Why that change of view on the part of Mr. Hearn, the defeated candidate, I do not know. It must surely have been represented to Mr. Hearn that Mr. McCloskey had been a faithful supporter of his in the election of 1911. I do not know what the reasons were, but I do not think I am far afield in supposing that that was the motive which induced him to change his recommendation. In May, immediately following Mr. Hearn's recommendation, the citizens of Wakaw became aware that that recommendation had been made, and the board of trade sent a strong protest to the department against Mr. McCloskey's appointment on the ground that he was not a fit person to hold the position of postmaster of the village; certain allegations of improper conduct, while he was acting in the capacity of teacher in a school in the vicinity having been made. The deputy took the proper step of wiring to the inspector to suspend Mr. MoClos-key's appointment until the protest of the board of trade had been given proper consideration, and an investigation had been held. On the 29th of May, the department wrote to Mr. Hearn, the defeated candidate, informing him of the protest of the board of trade against Mr. McCloskey's appointment, and asking him to further advise them. In the same month, not only the board of trade, but the citizens generally of Wakaw, sent a petition asking to have Mr. MoCloskey's appointment cancelled. Seventy-eight people signed the petition, everyone of whom was sworn in the presence of a notary in the village. During the same month, the department received a letter from the inspector at Saskatoon, advising them that he had received serious complaints against Mr. McCloskey to the effect that he was not a fit person for the position. The depart-

ment then notified Mr. Hearn of the petition and protest, and sent him the inspector's report on the matter. After the protest against Mr. McCloskey's appointment had been referred to Mr. Hearn for consideration and further advice, no reply came from Mr. Hearn. In the month of June he was notified that the board of trade had again petitioned for the appointment of this woman as postmistress, instead of Mr. McCloskey as postmaster. In July the department wrote to Mr. Hearn asking him for further advice as to Mr. McCloskey. In August the member for Prince Albert (Mr. McKay) became somewhat interested, because Wakaw is in the northwest comer of the constituency adjoining that of my hon. friend from Prince Albert, and I think my hon. friend is fairly well acquainted with the people of the village. He wrote to the department asking why Mr. McCloskey had not been appointed. This was in August. The department replied to the hon. member for Prince Albert informing him that they had received complaints against Mr. MoClos-key,' that he was not a fit person to hold the position of postmaster, and giving him details of the complaints. On the 21st ol August, the department again wrote to Mr. Hearn. You can see, Mr. Chairman, that during all the summer months of last year, the department refused to act upon the recommendation of the board of trade or upon the petition sent by practically every citizen in this village in favour of the appointment of a proper person to act as postmistress. They allowed the post office service to be utterly demoralized at that point, waiting month after month for the decision of the defeated candidate as to whether or not he still wished to recommend Mt. McCloskey for the position. In the latter part of August, the department again wrote to Mr. Hearn regarding the appointment, and he replied stating that he had consulted with the member for Prince Albert and asking the department, notwithstanding the complaints that had been entered against McCloskey, to go on and make the appointment. Then, early in September, the department wrote to the post office inspector Instructing him to carry out Mr. McCloskey's appointment and to install him as postmaster in the village, and I believe the inspector carried out those instructions and Mr. McCloskey was appointed. Later in the month, further serious complaints having been made to the inspector at Saskatoon, with reference to the character of this man who was appointed, that inspector was sent to inquire into the complaints, and he made a report to the effect that the people had absolutely no confidence in Mr. McCloskey as a person to hold the office. As a matter of fact, a
great many of the citizens were compelled to change their post office address, and to have their mail sent by special couriers to outlying post offices, rather than trust their mail in the hands of this person against whom the department had been warned, not only by the people of the village, but by the inspector who had investigated the matter on the ground, and who had found out for himself that the complaints were well founded. During this same month, the residents of the village again protested to the department against McCloskey's appointment, and on the 23rd of October, the assistant deputy postmaster general wrote on behalf of the department to Mr. Hearn telling him of the continued serious complaints against the postmaster. In November, Mr. Hearn wrote to the department confirming his former recommendation of Mr. McCloskey, and expressing the hope that no change would be made. That was a strange situation, Mr Chairman, that the people of that district should be compelled to accept the recommendation of the defeated candidate of Humboldt, a man who was something like 1,000 votes short of saving his deposit at the last election, should be compelled to accept the appointment of a man as to whose suitability he could not very well know personally, or only to a limited extent. I say it was a strange thing that his recommendation should be taken against the repeated protests of the citizens of the village and of the inspector himself, who, I assume, is no partisan, and who gave the department the results of his impartial investigation into the mat-
Fortunately for the people, the appointment did not last very long. This postmaster was arrested in the month of December on the streets for disorderly conduct, conduct unbecoming to any decent citizen, and he was brought before the magistrate in the village and fined. Other serious charges were laid against him and amongst them was the charge of a patron of the office who brought a certain sum of money to the post office, gave it into the hands of this gentleman, who claimed he had no money orders in his possession, and gave his own personal cheque which was worthless to this individual with the result that the patron of the office was defrauded by this postmaster out of $88 which he desired to send to Winnipeg or some other place to meet some business liability.
Does he still hold the office?	*

He held the office until he voluntarily skipped out of the country when charges were preferred against him, one by his wife of assault and the other by the clergyman of the church which he attended, when he did attend church, also

of assault. With these charges pending against him and the mounted police on the way to secure his person, this worthy appointee, recommended by my opponent in the last election, saw fit to decamp leaving the post office to take care of itself.
I have no fault to find with the Postmaster General for accepting, or appealing to the defeated candidate in Humboldt for his advice in reference to an appointment of this sort. But surely the Postmaster General should not have put the citizens of this village to the inconvenience of a practical suspension of the postal service for a whole year awaiting the pleasure of this gentleman, or until he should make up his mind who was the proper person to fill the office, but the appointment should have been made immediately. In the second place, I do not think that the advice of the defeated candidate or anybody else should induce the Postmaster General to make an appointment when charges as serious as those which were made against this individual are laid before a minister because that is the time when the Postmaster General ought to assert his authority and say to the defeated candidate or to the member representing the constituency: We cannot appoint that man, our information is that he is not a fit and proper person and therefore we would ask you to recommend somebody else. Notwithstanding this information, these reports from the inspector and these protests from other citizens of the village, the Postmaster General appoints this man. The next thing after his appointment that we know is that he is arrested on the street, fined for disorderly conduct and, very serious charges having been made against him, he finds it necessary to give up his office and skip out of the country so as to elude the mounted police who are on his trail, and who are endeavouring to secure his person and make him suffer the penalty of his misdeeds. That is the case which has been brought to my attention by the people of the district repeatedly and I have awaited this opportunity to bring the matter before the Postmaster General. Surely the Postmaster General could not have had a matter like that brought to his ersonal attention; otherwise, he would not ave carried out the recommendation of the defeated candidate and appointed a man of this character. Yet, on the other hand,
I maintain that whatever be the practice the department follows in making appointments, it is not fair to the people, it is not fair to the public service, that the people should be deprived of a proper postal service for months and months simply awaiting the pleasure of the man who happened to be the Government candidate in the elections. There is surely no reason why the whole community should suffer the penalty of his delay and inaction in making a proper recommendation to the department.
