The documents in connection with Mr. Lyster's dismissal and the position of the postmaster constitute a very interesting comment on the methods that are evidently being adopted and pursued in the Post Office Department in reference to these dismissals. It appears that a complaint was sent to the Postmaster General some time in October, 1911, that Mr. Lyster was an active partisan, that he should be compelled to resign from his office and that another gentleman should be appointed in his place. This protest was sent to the minister by two gentlemen by the name of Hill and Daly, president and secretary, respectively, of the Lloydminster Conservative Association. In the month of December, these gentlemen wrote again to the Postmaster General asking him that the matter of dismissing Mr. Lyster be left for the time being in abeyance. I would be obliged if you would favour me with your further instructions in regard to-holding the judicial inquiry as to the charges made against N. S. Lyster, postmaster at Lloydminster. Eeferring to our letter of the 16th December, asking that the dismissal of Mr. Lyster be left in abeyance, we would be glad if you could carry out the recommendation of our letter of 27th .November that Mr. Lyster be dismissed and George M. Mayberry appointed in his stead, and that the dismissal be carried out without the formality of an inquiry.
That is a good Tory method. That was the second request for the dismissal of Mr. Lyster. It does not look as if these gentlemen had any serious complaints to make against him. Just as soon as the citizens of Lloydminster heard of what had happened, they sent in a petition, signed by no less than three hundred and fifty of the patrons of this office, protesting against the removal of Mr. Lyster as postmaster, and stating that he had given the very best service to the community. These three hundred and fifty names probably represent the great majority of the supporters of both political parties; certainly they are not confined to supporters of the Liberal party. The gentleman who forwarded this petition, stated that it had not been circulated, but had been left in one place, and that the people had come and signed it voluntarily. Notwithstanding this protest, the defeated candidate in that district, Mr. Howell, who lives in the town of North Battleford, became mixed up in the matter and also urged the dismissal of Mr. Lyster. He sent Mr. Keith, a Conservative lawyer of North Battleford, to Lloydminster to conduct the investigation. On the file appears the evidence taken by Mr. Keith at that inquiry and also his recommendation to the department. I just want to show that, even when the Postmaster General undertakes these fair, impartial investigations, he does not always hold himself to be bound by them. This is the letter sent by Mr. Keith to the Postmaster General, summing up the result of his investigation:

Hall, and Ivan Frederick Crossley, both of whom stated that Mr. Lyster was around the Lloyminster polling booth on the last Dominion election day for part of the day, but neither of them would state that he was taking any part in the election proceedings. I said at the outset that I was not complaining of dismissals in my own constituency, though ,a number of dismissals have been made. But let the Postmaster General tell us that the position is that if he finds out that a man has Mr. NEELY.
Liberal leanings in his heart, whether he expresses them or not, he is going to be fired from public office, if that office is in the Post Office Department. If the minister will say that we shall know where we stand and the .country will know what he means and how he intends to carry on his department. Some of the dismissals-and the two I have selected are among the number-are certainly altogether unworthy of a great department of the Government which we have looked upon in the past as probably more free from partisan manipulation and control than any other department of the Government.

As to the first case the hon. gentleman referred to, I am getting the thick file which we have in the department put in brief form in order to be able to speak about the matter when the supplementary estimates are taken up. As to the postma'stership of Lloydminster, I had enough trouble about that to remember something of it. The view I take is that if the commissioner in holding an investigation does not take down or have taken down, notes of the evidence, his report is binding; I have no power to go over it even if I wanted to,-which I never did. But if evidence has been taken down and is placed before me, and if I am satisfied on reading that evidence that 'the commissioner has made a mistake either in favour of the postmaster or against him, I will give my own judgment on the evidence. The .commissioner is only the representative of the Postmaster General for the purpose of holding an investigation; he is not the man who decides whether the postmaster remains or not; that is the duty of the postmaster himself. I read the evidence in this case, and it seemed to me that the proof had been made. My judgment may be good or it may be bad. But the hon. gentleman is wrong when he says that it suffices for a man to have Liberal leanings to be dismissed. In my own county there are forty-five or fifty postmasters, not ten per cent of whom are Conservatives; and out of the whole, only two have been dismissed for political partisanship.
There have been more in other counties, but this rule which has been followed in my county will show my hon. friends opposite that they should not be surprised when these Liberal postmasters are dismissed.	.
Mr. .1. DEMERS (St. John and Iberville); Mr. Chairman, the Post Office Department has sent Mr. Joseph Barsalou, the mail carrier in the city of St. John, a notice stating that his contract would expire on the 16th of August next, whereas it should not expire before April, 1915. I wish to know from the hon. Postmaster General

what reasons the department can allege for putting an end to this contract?
We shall take note of this, and I shall give my hon. friend that information.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
speechtext:
To the average mind there might appear to be a possibility that the newspaper and other reports have been unfair to the Postmaster General. 1 am always prepared to believe that in the criticism of their actions, public men are not always fairly dealj with, that any slip which they make may be somewhat exaggerated, and that when we get at the real facts they are not so bad as they appear on the surface. The reverse of that situation, however is altogether true in respect of the department of the Postmaster. I have had a great deal to do with the department of the Postmaster .General during the last 12 or 15 years. I never received any favours from that department, and I am not aware that I ever asked for any. I represent a very large constituency, in which there are a great many mail contracts. I am in the presence of the officials of the Postmaster General, and I ask them to speak out if they can say that I ever asked the Postmaster General to do the slightest 'favour to anyone aside from acting on the principle of accepting the lowest tender. The lowest tenderer got the contract every time, and if any gentleman who was tendering made any inquiries with regard to the matter, the invariable answer was: Things are done in an honest way in the Post Office Department; if you are the lowest tenderer you will get the contract. That is the treatment the public would expect to receive at the hands of the Postmaster General. I heard the Postmaster General this afternoon talking about a certain character in ancient history known as Ananias, and he characterized some of his opponents as being connected with that particular sort of humanity. If the hon. Postmaster General exhausted his comparisons, and had nothing left with which he himself could be compared, I would remind him that Ananias left a widow. The Holy Book points out that when Ananias fell dead, his wife came in a few moments afterwards, not knowing that she was a widow. She also lied before the Lord, and she also fell dead. The Postmaster General had better be careful, for, if he does not bear any relationship to 'Ananias, he may be found to have a striking resemblance to his widow. The hon. gentleman talks about trials and about evidence; the idea, he says, asking the Post Office Department or the Postmaster General to be governed by evidence is absurd. The hon. gentleman went back
to the days of Ananias, and there found something upon which to base his comparisons. I wish to refer him and those of his followers who are fond of quoting cases and precedents to the fact that in the old day there was a court in or about the very same place which is brought to the mind by the reference of my hon. friend to ancient history. In that court there sat a distinguished jurist known as Pilate. He found that there was no evidence, but that had nothing to do with his decision, and he reached the conclusion that he had to play to the mob. My hon. friend the Postmaster General finds that there is no evidence; he has got a mob to play to, and he must, Pilate-like, give a decision to please that mob. Not only has he a mob to play to, but invariably he has his Barabas who must be relieved from poverty and put in a position of affluence. So we have the widow of Ananias as to facts, we have the Pilate as to the court and the evidence, we have the same old mob to cater to, and the Barabbas who has to be relieved. I notice that the Postmaster General was delighted this afternoon in the thought that he had discovered something to say against the ex-Postmaster General, ttie bon. member for Rouville. But I am afraid the hon. Postmaster General exploded too soon. He thought he had found something upon which he could create a scandal, or find fault of some substantial character in respect of the ex-Postmaster General, but on the slightest investigation it turns out that there was nothing behind this storm and fury. When I was sitting here and watching the veheminance and eruptions and explosions of the Postmaster General, I could not help thinking of an old Scotch preacher who had come down from the Highlands to visit a small Gaelic-speaking congregation in London. On the way down he stayed with a brother preacher, who asked him to preach in English to his congregation. This he seldom did, and then not very well, but he did not like to refuse, and he accordingly consented. He took as his text: 'The devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about seeking whom he may devour.' In opening his address he said: My brethren, I want to deal with this text under three headings; who the devil he was, where the devil he was going, and wfoat the devil he was roaring at. That is the way I felt about this tremendous explosion of the Postmaster General. What was the trouble, what did he explode about? What did he do about the contract? He had the opportunity, according to tihe best legal opinion we could get here in the House to-night, and it was not contradicted. The hon. member for Welland, who is regarded as a clearheaded lawyer, gave him an opinion on this contract which he accepted. He said

that opinion is good, I have no quarrel with it. It was that he could have cancelled that contract. What did he do? He ratified the contract although he could have cancelled it and he added another clause to it and is willing to carry it forward in its fulness. He says there was a very dangerous clause in it that the contract had to be filled ' substantially ' in order to get an extension for a further period. He changes that, saying it is poor legal phraseology and he says ' properly.' That is the result of this ponderous investigation and the product of the brain of my hon. friend. He said it was a tremendous thing that this country should be submitted to this contract as it passed the hands of the department in the first instance. I was watching him here to-night as I would have watched Pilate of old if I had had an opportunity of watching Pilate when he had given his decision, when he had catered to his mob and satisfied his Barabbas. He had his officials around him and when one basket after another' was placed before him, with the gruesome heads in it, with the blood streaming off them, freezing on the basket, he delighted over them and laughed to his officials: Are we not doing splendidly? That is the. hon. gentleman who is supposed to be representing the King in connection with this contract. I have a copy of the contract here. As I said the other night, the Prime Minister, when he was first returned to power, said that his victory was not a party victory but a national victory.
He meant Nationalist.

That may be. We
would expect the several departments which are under the general control of the Prime Minister to act according to this principle and this extreme bitter partisanship could not be expected. Here we have a contract signed by Mr. Louis Phillipe Pelletier, K.C., Postmaster General of Canada, acting for and on behalf of His Majesty the King. He dismissed this man down in Quebec on no evidence at all. The man was supposed to have carried a newspaper in his pocket and to have passed it to somebody in an election, although of that there is no evidence. He had only an extra judicial oath which is contrary to law, at least in my province, and in spite of that he breaks a solemn contract given for four years. There was not a particle of evidence to show that this man did not do everything he was required to do under the contract which he had entered into after competition and public tender. I ask hon. gentlemen if they are proud of their national victory, proud of being the representatives of the King, when a poor man in this Mr. McKENZIE.
country cannot compete for a contract and perform that contract to the letter, relying on .the principle that the King can do no wrong; but is thrown to the wolves, his	contract is	cancelled
and he has no remedy whatever. The poorest man in the land, when he enters into a contract, has his remedies if that contract is violated. But I submit we are taking cowardly advantage of the name of the King, and, sheltering ourselves behind it, in breaking contracts every day simply to cater to the mob and to make room for a new Barabbas every time. A Pilate is at the head of it all, for the Postmaster General is the guiltiest of the guilty in connection with these matters. He is the Radeliffe of the Tory party; that is giving him a character which he deserves. I have had other cases in my own county, but when I heard of the cases from Antigonish, where tenders were asked for and some of them were 'lower than those which obtained the contracts, and when I find letters going out of the office of the Postmaster General asking some heeler in the county of Antigonish to devise some miserable scheme by which they could outwit the lowest tenderer and give the contract to another, it is so far beyond anything that happened in my county that I am not going to say anything more about it. I am not exaggerating this. The letters were read here to-night, and they are on file. They were most shocking to me, because I never thought that anything could happen in the Post Office Department which would prevent an honest man who put in the lowest tender from getting the contract. We have heard the cases of two men who were turned down, and both of them were lower in their tenders than the men who got the contract, and all by reason of the fact that some Tory heeler in Antigonish wrote to the Postmaster General. What further evidence is required, and what more can we expect? Is there any member who will now write to his constituents and say that the honest, clean thing is being done in the Post Office Department, that if you are the lowest tenderer you will get the contract? There is no hope for that now. What we will have to say is: do not tender at all; or if you do, get into some conniving scheme with' a Tory heeler in order that you may get into this Pilate's court which caters to the mob, and perhaps a Barabbas will get it, and you will get it under him. That is the machinery that is provided now in the Post Office Department. Let us hope that the cancer is confined to this department, and that the Prime Minister will see that the yellow flag is put on the door, and that the people-

will keep away from that poisonous, pestiferous institution where nothing honest can be done. Let me advise the minister to put the yellow flag there, and to see that the disease does not spread to other departments.

Are the
salaries of any of the assistant postmasters in the larger cities, such as Halifax, being increased?
We are trying to fix that.
May I expect that the hon. gentleman will bring down the complete file relating to this stamp vending machine contract?
The moment the hon. gentleman requested it, I gave orders that it be done.
When may I expect it?

As soon as it is
copied. I have given instructions to have it done without delay.
May I expect it on Monday or Tuesday?
Monday.
I would like to see the original contract.
I will bring it down.

My hon. friend from
Richmond wishes an opportunity to bring up one or two cases when the supple-mentaries are considered.

I told him it would
be all right.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions, $1,916,934.

Are we to take these
and the Trade and Commerce items on the last page, too?
We could leave one item in each, so that any question could be asked by hon. gentlemen later, if they wish.

I would like to bring
up the question of the Paris agency. Is that in the Prime Minister's estimates?

speechtext: Yes.
When can I take it up?

speechtext: When the supplement-aries come up.

We can let item 168 of
the Mail Subsidies stand.
Steam service between Halifax and Sherbrooke, $2,000.

Will the minister tell
me the ports of call between Halifax and Sherbrooke? .

The ports of call are Port Dufferin and Moser river, in Halifax county and Ecum-Secum, Marie-Joseph, Liscomb and Sonora in Guysborough county.
Steam service from the opening to the^ closing of navigation in 1913, between Pictou, Mulgrave and Cheticamp, $7,500.
Who is the contractor?

The contractor is the
same man as last year, Captain W. A. Beattie.
What is the cause of the increase?

He gets $7,000 and there is a small service to be performed for $500 between Pictou and Mulgrave calling _ at some of the smaller places. I have forgotten the contractor for this service, but I can get it for my hon. . friend.
Referring to the larger service to be performed by Captain Beattie, does the boat call at ports in Antigonish?

It makes a round trip
every fortnight between Mulgrave and Pictou, and two round trips each week between Mulgrave and Cheticamp, calling both ways at Port Hastings, Port Hawkes-bury, Port Hood, Margaree harbour, Grand Etang, Eastern harbour and Big Pond, and calling once each week at Pleasant bay.

Then this boat will
not call at any ports in Antigonish?
The places that the minister has named are in Inverness county.

The boat going from
Pictou to Mulgrave will call, I understand, at several points in Antigonish.

The boat running from
Pictou to Mulgrave calls both ways at Arisag, Georgeville, Cape George, Morristown, Malignant Cove, Livingstone Cove, Ballantyne Cove and Cribbin's Point.

Why do you reduce
the frequency of calls there?
As I have explained, we are putting on a smaller boat. I am sorry I have not got its itinerary, but my hon. friend can get it in the department. This smaller boat will make trips also from Pictou.
Is it a motor boat or a steamer?
It is an auxiliary gasoline schooner.

I am not complaining of the smaller boat service. I think it is proper, but I do think that once a fortnight is cutting out that shore pretty badly where they have no railway communication. With the increasing revenues of the Government there is no reason why there should not be a boat calling at Arisaig, Cape George, and Morristown once a week. .
We had much trouble arranging this service and thought we could meet the requirements by reducing the number of trips of the large boat and putting on an additional small boat.

It may be that the
manner in which these harbours were neglected during the last two years has impressed the Government with the difficulty of calling as regularly as the needs of the people require and I suppose that is why this smaller service has been put on. I hope the Government will see that these harbours are dredged and that the boat will be able to call at them regularly.
Steam service between Pictou and Montague and between Charlottetown and Montague, calling at Murray Harbour and Georgetown, $6,900.
This service has been altered a little and the description is not correct. I move that the words ' and between Charlottetown and Montague ' be struck out.

Amendment agreed to.
Steam service between Prince Edward Island and Cape Breton and Newfoundland, $12,000.

What is the name of
the steamer that is performing this service and where does she call in Cape Breton?
This service is carried on by the Dominion Coal Company. The steamers start from Montreal and call at Summerside and Charlottetown and in Cape Breton and North Sydney and Sydney.

Yes, I am familiar
with the service.

Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved second reading of Bill No 231, to amend the Customs Tariff.

When addressing the House on the budget debate, I discussed the question of the small reduction in duties which were made upon raw sugar by reason of the West Indian agreement and the Customs Tariff Act. I stated at that time that it would not assist the consumer to any great extent, because all the sugar refiners in Canada were in the combine. I have since been informed that one refining com-Mr. PERLEY.
pany, the Dominion Sugar Company, Limited, was not actually in the combine. I am told that they sell direct to the retailer. I do not wish to mis-state any position and I take this opportunity of making these remarks.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
Bill considered in committee, reported, read the third time and passed.
